utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Therefore, we'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. We left off yesterday, I was asking you about your specialty. I was able to see some of your military gazettes last night which for your promotions noted you as an infantry officer. So that's right, isn't it, you're an infantry man?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question? Not just nodding. We need it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the answer out loud --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we still do not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The translation is ongoing all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't replied because I was waiting for the interpreter to conclude. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- we'll go to July 1995 now, and your statement which is our number D1203 notes that you were interviewed by Milenko Dundjer on 12 July 2014. And did you speak to Mr. Dundjer or any other member of the Defence about these events of your wedding, about the material in your report, prior to 12 July 2014?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your wife's report, D1202, shows us the date of 12 July 2014 for her interview with Mr. Dundjer, and -- but it also says that -- she had an interview on the 10th of January, 2012. And I take it you've for -- prior to seeing Mr. Dundjer on the 14th -- excuse me. The 12th of July, 2014, you had a chance to speak to your wife to -- about the subject matter that Mr. Dundjer questioned her about in 2012?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it have to do whether my wife had seen Mr. Dundjer before? Is that what you were trying to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. My question was did you -- well, did you have a chance to talk to your wife about the subject matter that she talked to Dundjer about in 2012?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need, since it involved our wedding. We certainly knew what the date of our wedding was, even without Mr. Dundjer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was not whether there was any need to discuss it. Did you discuss with your wife what she discussed in 2012 when being interviewed? Did you speak with her about the questions that were asked to her? And whether there was a need to do that is not something that is of any interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss it in this context. We only discussed the possibility of both of us appearing as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let me take you to the context that -- well, from my perspective. General Mladic has been, in 2012, arrested. He's going to soon be on trial. Your wife is interviewed by a Defence investigator and is -- provides information obviously about the events on the day of your wedding. This was in 2012. Surely, sir, after your wife -- or before your wife speaks to this investigator in this utmost serious topic you're going to talk with your wife about what the investigator asked her and about what she said. It's what husbands and wives do. So you talked to your wife about what the investigator had asked her about, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: We mostly discussed the possibility of our appearing as witnesses at Mr. Mladic's trial, relating to the events that we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the first sentence of your question: "General Mladic has been, in 2012, arrested." Are you sure that this date is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I meant to say he been arrested and I believe he had been arrested by that time, but I may be wrong. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it, that you just referred to a time-frame in which Mr. Mladic had already been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and -- perhaps the witness could answer the question now directly. Because you said what you mostly discussed. The question was whether you also discussed the questions that were put to your wife and what she said in 2012.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a question for clarification. What triggered the discussion between your wife and yourself to discuss the possibility of you becoming witnesses in this case? What was the reason had you to discuss the fact that you may be called as witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't remember. Thank you so much. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, before your statement in 2014, you did have a chance to speak with your wife about some of the events at the wedding, specifically when General Mladic arrived, how long he stayed, that kind of thing. There's nothing wrong with that, sir. You can talk with your wife to help refresh her recollection. So didn't you talk with your wife to help each other refresh your recollection about when General Mladic came and how long he stayed? Didn't you do that before your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We both knew the sequence of events. There was no need to try to harmonise things in detail or discuss the matter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't suggest harmonise. I said help refresh your recollection. So is your answer that you didn't talk to your wife before you talked to the investigator to help refresh your recollection about what happened when Mladic came, how long he stayed?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, my wife and I discussed the matter with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you've mentioned before, what you did mostly or for the most part is not very helpful. So can you acknowledge now that you and your wife did talk about the details of when Mladic arrived, how long he stayed, before you spoke to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you spoke to the investigator, was your wife with you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my interview with the investigator, she was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during her interview with the investigators, were you with her?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the restaurant. And what time do you recall General Mladic arriving at the restaurant on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to say that I already said yesterday that we left our apartment together for the church. We were together at the church throughout the wedding ceremony and after that, again all of us, including ourselves, General Mladic and the guests --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for one reason or another you think we're interested in things not asked. The question -- can you hear me through the interpretation? If you'd just focus on what is asked -- but any problem on the B/C/S channel? Not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please answer the question. For one reason or another, you think that we're interested in things we're not asking you, or Mr. McCloskey is not asking you. At what time, as far as you remember, did Mr. Mladic arrive at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise if I was misunderstood. That was not my intention. I simply wanted to summarise something I had already said. But do allow me to provide a direct answer to Mr. Prosecutor's question. General Mladic, ourselves, and the guests, once the wedding ceremony was over, around 2.00, we arrived at the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say "around 2.00." So given that had happened almost -- well, when you first started -- when your wife was first asked about it in 2012, it happened a long time ago before you started talking about it. So when you say "around 2.00," would that give or take an hour, give or take 30 minutes? What's your best "around" estimate?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So give or take an hour is fair, given the time distance and the memory issues?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour would be too much. And I don't think it was before 2.00. I don't think we arrived at the restaurant before 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were you able to remember it was around 2.00? Because it's not in your statement. Just now?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked about the time. I know that the wedding ceremony had been scheduled to take place between noon and 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So it's based on your memory of the wedding schedule, not the actual time you arrived there? Which is fair enough. Even I remember the time of my wedding. Okay. I'm sorry, I was talking and so they probably didn't hear your answer. Let me just continue then, I think. Can you tell us that -- now, at the restaurant, was this a sit-down meal, or was it one of these buffet affairs where people get their meals at the buffet and sit around at tables, or was this a more formal, everybody sits down at one table and gets served?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a wedding lunch, meaning the people were seated at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you first got to the restaurant, were there -- was there a like a small gathering in another room where people had perhaps drinks or snacks then got together before they actually sat down? Or did people, were they invited into the restaurant and sat down at the table?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once they entered the restaurant, they sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there music played at the restaurant once people sat down, or before?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Music began after they were seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- do you remember roughly how long after people were seated that the music started?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but I know that the musicians stayed until 8.00 p.m., for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's how long they stayed, but my question was how long after people sat down at the table did the music start playing.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there drinks served at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Wine?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Beer?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did General Mladic have his share of those drinks, any of those?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to make the toast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the last item on the drinking list is not there because you spoke too early.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Slivovitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we best get the slivovitz at the wedding on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on there now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what beverage did General Mladic use in his toast?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what beverage were you drinking at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any slivovitz?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only at the beginning, to join the toast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I take it over this long evening of your wedding, you had a few drinks and you were feeling good -- good about the day.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are in charge of organising things, you have to bear in mind your conduct, no matter how much you drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree, but let's get how much you did drink. Did you drink enough so you could feel the alcohol?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Did you have a chance to dance with your bride at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time were you able to dance with your bride?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. It depended on the music.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at the time you were dancing with your wife, you -- General Mladic could have gone up and -- and left the area to the restroom for a few minutes, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not without me noticing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did General Mladic ever leave during this period of time from 2.00 p.m. to 5.30 and go to the restroom?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, did he get up and take a break and go outside ever to -- or your eyes were on him the entire time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was before me throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to a photo that the Defence provided us of your wedding. It's 32879. And if Ms. Stewart could put it in, in Sanction I think we might get a clearer picture of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up I would like to ask a question for the witness. Mr. Stojkovic, did anybody smoke during the long dinner or lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you mean in the room or outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the people were smoking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to move away from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were asked to move a little away from the microphone because it's difficult for the interpreters to listen. I understand the people were smoking in the dining-room; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did General Mladic smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before we continue, I'd like to put a few questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I correct a misstatement I made just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We haven't seen it yet, but we are about to see a photograph that actually was not provided by the Defence. We picked it up ourselves so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have two short questions. How did you move from the apartment to the church? Did you walk? Were you in cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We walked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you move from the church to the restaurant? Did you walk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also. We walked, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at this photograph, if we can; 65 ter 32879. Do you see that photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it'll come up. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record we see General Mladic near the centre of the photograph. It appears to be a cigarette in his left hand, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But since I was a smoker myself, I didn't pay any attention to one cigarette in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we've seen General Mladic smoking in the Hotel Fontana while speaking to people. So we know he smokes more than just one cigarette at one wedding. Are you suggesting this was the only cigarette General Mladic had at your wedding, your wedding dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. You really can't be sure how many cigarettes General Mladic smoked or how many times he went to the restroom, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for cigarettes, I cannot be sure. As for the restroom, I do know that he did not leave the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And is this a picture of your wedding dinner at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see your bride next to General Mladic, and then we see you as a slightly younger man with your hand to your chin?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we focus in a bit on General Mladic's watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it's not perfect, but if you look at your watch and you kind of tilt it like that, what time does that look like to you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought it looked more like 1400 hours. But it is fuzzy.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks like 1500 to me. Rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber is in a position to -- to analyse what the Chamber sees and we do understand that you consider it to be more 1500 hours and that the witness rather thinks as that -- the witness rather thinks that it's 1500 hours and you think it's rather 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes but I don't intend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to take it any further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to show you one thing to see if it will refresh your recollection. You're a military man. General Mladic was a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go, as the last exhibit, Mr. President -- I would offer this into evidence and I don't know if the Court wants the blow-up or wants -- I think you can probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once it is in evidence, the Chamber and the Judges, Mr. McCloskey, believe it or not, are able to zoom in and out. And if there's any expert better matter of looking at that time, then please present that, but just zooming in and out is within our competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Your Honour knows I -- well, I think I know you're playing with me, so I take it as that. But if you ever need Ms. Stewart's and Sanction's help to do what we did in court today we're always at your service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could -- I'd offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it uploaded into e-court. It is, Madam Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32879 receives Exhibit P7511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question for the witness. Did I understand you well, that on from when you met - I think that was at 10.00 in the morning - up to the time Mr. Mladic left the restaurant which covers a time of approximately seven to eight hours that neither you nor he went to the restroom. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean irrespective of the wedding dinner? You are referring to the entire period from 10.00 a.m. at the apartment onwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you want to split it up, that's fine. If you say I saw him going to the restroom in the apartment or during the ceremony in church, that's fine. But you said you didn't lose him out of sight during that whole period so that's the reason why I'm asking it for the whole period. But if you can be more specific, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was not from 10.00 a.m. onwards. It was about the meal in the dining-room, and that's why I said that we were in the dining-room all the time in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm now extending that question where your statements says that you're always with him and you didn't lose him out of sight from when he arrived. Could you tell us, neither you nor he did go to the restroom when you were in the restaurant. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, from 12.00 to 2.00, you said it was the ceremony in church. You walked there. You walked from there to the restaurant. Did you or he go to the restroom during those two hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Since that is not allowed during the church ceremony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, from 10.00 to 12.00, from the moment he arrived at your apartment and up to the moment where you arrived at the church, Walking there, did you or he go to the restroom during those two hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall exactly. Probably. Since it's a small apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether in a small apartment you go more to the restroom and in a large apartment, so leave that aside. So you say you don't know whether you or he went to the restroom between 10.00 and 12.00 but from 12.00 to anywhere between 5.00 and 6.00 up to the moment that Mr. Mladic left the restaurant you, neither he, did go to the restroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, are you sure about it; or do you say, Well, it may have been but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, that's the way it was. I cannot express myself in any other way: As far as I can remember, after all, there is a time-period involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one question. Sir, at the restaurant -- I'm talking to you. At the restaurant, did you -- did anybody else other than Mr. Mladic go to the restroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say probably because you didn't observe anybody going to the restroom. You don't remember observing anybody going to the restroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember since I was sitting at the head table, and there were about 80 people present all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And quite possibly some people went to the restroom without you noticing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Except for those who sat at the head table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but there was dancing at a certain time, isn't it so, and the people sitting at the head table sort of spread around and started dancing. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... at that time, you would have been dancing with your wife and concentrating on the dance with your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in those circumstances anybody on the dance floor could have gone to the bathroom without you noticing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the dance floor, one could see the head table the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there's nobody at the head table. Everybody's on the dance floor. I'm asking the question during that dancing anybody could have gone to the bathroom without you noticing. You were concentrating on the dance with your wife. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the question had to do with General Mladic, who did not dance, and he was sitting at the head table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic did not dance? Is that your testimony? He sat at the head table right through the dinner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it help your recollection if I told you we've seen General Mladic's home videos at weddings. He's quite a dancer. Doesn't that help you remember that he liked to dance at weddings and he actually danced at your wedding?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Is this photo -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One short question. Where in this restaurant was the restroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Outside the dining-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On which floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What floor is the restaurant itself? On what floor is the restaurant itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same one where the dining-room is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on what floor is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or the floor in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In between what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the apartment building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am completely lost now. I don't understand your answer, sir. I'm not -- the floor in between the apartment building. The apartment building and what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The restaurant and its dining-room are located within an apartment building, and the restaurant and its dining-room are on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the toilet, the restroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise. Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's what I wanted to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and earlier you said "or the floor in between." Did you mean to say that there was a kind of a semi- or half floor or halfway the stairs from one floor to another, that it could have been there? If you don't remember, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was determining the floors in relation to height, so it is definitely the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just one last exhibit and a short series of questions. Could we go to P01338.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you're active lieutenant-colonel in the VJ. You've certainly heard of General Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We need to go to the next page. Sorry, this is the wrong one. P1338. Okay. Thank you. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your rank on the day of your wedding?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had you heard of -- on your wedding -- actually, I believe he was a colonel, Vinko Pandurevic, at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What we have in front of us here is an intercepted communication by the Bosnian State Security Service on 16 July 1995 at 1615 hours, the time that you were at the restaurant, and we see that this is between the Main Staff duty officer, and that means the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska who was located, at the time, in Crna Rijeka, and General Mladic. And they couldn't make out -- the intercepters couldn't make out General Mladic's part of the conversation. But we can see from the -- from what the duty officer is saying, he's giving information about the president called a short while ago and, in our view, that would be President Karadzic. He mentions Pandurevic, other officials, and what I was wondering if you take a careful look at this intercept, which the Prosecution believes, sir, is absolutely genuine, do you remember General Mladic mentioning anything to you about the goings-on over in Bosnia, anything about the president, anything about Pandurevic? Anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when General Mladic, he left the restaurant early; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1730 he said good-bye, and I saw him off at 1730.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but that was earlier than everyone else.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were people who left even earlier. They had to because of transportation since there were wedding guests who were coming in from outside Belgrade. There were some like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But is it fair to say he excused himself and cited official duties?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, when your wife testified, page 38058, starting at line 24 the question -- well, 20. Question says: "To the best of your knowledge, do you remember when General Mladic and his wife left your wedding?" And what she said was: "Yes. I think I pointed out in my statement it was around 5.30. I don't know whether it was a minute or two before or later, but definitely around 5.30 or quarter to 6.00. That is when he left the dining hall at the Dva Ribara restaurant where the ceremonial lunch took place. He excused himself, citing official duties." And I quote your wife: "He excused himself, citing official duties." And then she said: "I stayed in the dining hall with my guests while my husband escorted him to the car." So you would agree with your wife, would you not, that she's correct? Perhaps you didn't hear Mladic tell that to her, but she said he excused himself, citing official duties. So would you support your wife on that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about official duties, but I am sure that he excused himself and said good-bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have no reason to believe your wife is not telling the truth about that statement, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Since, when one leaves a wedding, one says good bye to the bride and the groom. So I do not rule out the possibility that that is what she was told, but I did not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have. No, I first give an opportunity -- any questions arising from cross, Mr. Lukic, which you'd like to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but can I consult with my client for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. But, again, it's not the first time that Mr. Mladic speaks at audible volume and that is the only thing he is not allowed to do. So take care that nothing can be heard by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day once again.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please let us focus now on the arrival in the Dva Ribara restaurant. You were asked whether it was an hour before or later, and you said it's around 2.00, not earlier. Can you say that an hour was too long? How much later? Can you tell us now? Five, ten minute, half an hour later?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, around 1400 hours, we left the church on foot towards the restaurants and that is why I said "around 1400 hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Question -- how far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the logical follow-up question is how far is it from the church to the restaurant, 500 metres, 200 metre, 1 kilometre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A couple of hundred metres. 500 metres maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it wouldn't take more than ten, 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, calculating already that walking in a wedding dress doesn't go as fast as in a normal dress. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had been put to you that the general liked to dance at parties. You told us that you do not remember that he danced. What happened in the Mladic family during that last year, a year and a bit, before your wedding? Did some misfortune befall the family?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened in the Mladic family?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lost their daughter, Ana.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you did not lose sight of the general. What kind of status does the best man enjoy in our part of the world?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best man, much like in the English culture, it entails someone of high moral principle, exemplary conduct, and family orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at the intercept before us, P1338. My colleague, Mr. McCloskey also said --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. McCloskey told you that those intercepting such conversations were unable to hear General Mladic in this case. In the intercept itself, among the words uttered by the participants, there's no mention of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At 4.15 on the day of your wedding, to the best of your recollection and to the best of your knowledge, would it have been possible for General Mladic to establish radio communication with the Main Staff of the VRS in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, let me just ask you this: Would you say you were drunk at your own wedding?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be all we had of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one or two questions for you, Mr. Stojkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A statement was taken from you and a statement was taken from your wife. Those statements were signed. Did you read or see the statement that was taken from your wife?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did your wife see or read your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of your own statement?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean here or before the trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At any time. If you did, tell us when.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not recall when or that you got a copy?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether I received one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any recollection as to giving your wife access to the statement that was put on paper for you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because, as far as I remember, our statements remained with the counsel to whom we had provided them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were finally prepared for appearing as a witness here, the statement of your wife was not shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement was shown to me when I arrived here during the proofing I had with Mr. Branko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you alone during that proofing or were you together with your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At times, I was together with my wife, depending on the attorney-at-law's, Mr. Branko Lukic's requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So during the part of the proofing, you were there and your wife was there as well.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you -- at that time, was your statement read to her or was her statement read to you, during that part of the proofing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the following reasons, and I'd like you to first listen to what I'm telling you. When your wife was asked at what time Mr. Mladic left the restaurant, she said: "As I said already in my statement, it was at 5.30." Now, in the statement of your wife that time is not mentioned. However, in your statement that time is mentioned. So I wondered why your wife said: "As you can see in my statement it was 5.30," where we can only see that in your statement. Do you have any explanation as to why she would have said: "As you can see in my statement, it was 5.30," where it is not in hers but it is in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO STOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a particular explanation, except for the fact that my wife knew the approximate time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm focussing not on the time. I'm focussing on what she said, that that can be found in his statement, which was not the case. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to make sure I heard you properly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Sit down. Sit down. Mr. Mladic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still can hear Mr. Mladic so he should really speak at inaudible volume or remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. You may want to look at paragraph 9 of the wife's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you do that, can I ask the question I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I made a mistake, of course, I stand to be corrected, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should be D1202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. You said paragraph ... Yes, it says "about." Where -- I do agree that I -- it -- that it could be understood as mentioning 5.30 and I stand, in that respect, corrected. And that's -- it's good that you point my attention to it. I was looking at the figures, 5.30, is in the statement of the husband whereas approximately that time is mentioned in the statement of the wife. I stand corrected. I think I have not sufficiently looked at that. And if that is what Mr. Mladic wanted to bring to the attention of Mr. Stojanovic, then I better understand -- then I better understand why he wanted to intervene immediately. That's on the record hereby. I think Mr. Mladic wanted to convey something else. You can tell it to Mr. Stojanovic if there's anything you would like to bring to our attention. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I also thank Mr. McCloskey for pointing at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted one question. Just to make sure I heard you properly, did I hear you correctly that you said when you were with Mr. Lukic together with your wife at the same time, that was at Mr. Lukic's request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that procedurally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please finish what you started saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that it was at Mr. Lukic's request so as to explain to us the procedure and protocols in place before the Tribunal when it comes to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojkovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were -- all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, at least I got a note, that we had received information that there were no further witnesses available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we expected the problems last week and we have the problems now apparently. When will the next witness arrive and when --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next witness should arrive on Saturday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any explanation as to why this situation arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a scheduled videolink from Banja Luka but Banja Luka court is not operating before the 25th of August, so we were not able to organise that videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen that. But no other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No other witnesses were able to come before the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's for a fact we can't go on the streets and find witnesses and fill our time. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one issue to raise if we are going to finish the day for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we are not because we have a lot of items on our agenda to be read --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we are already late for the break and we should have stopped 15 minutes ago. We take a break, and I suggest that we take a break for half an hour and we resume after that. Any matter you'd like to raise then is -- you could do that first and after that we'll deal with quite a few procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just asked by Mr. Mladic if it is possible for him to leave and not to be present for these procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic always can waive his right to be -- to be present during trial. Whether he can be transported immediately is a matter that's beyond our control, but at least the Registry is now aware of the wish of Mr. Mladic to -- to not further attend. We'll -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to proceed, not having received yet any written waiver, I'd like to have Mr. Mladic, at this moment, confirm orally that he waives his right to be present after the break just for this day. If he could use the microphone to tell us, then we would have it on the record. Mr. Mladic, do you waive your right to attend court for the rest of this day in which we'll not hear any further evidence but in which we'll deal with procedural matters. Could you please respond to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Comrade Orie, I waive my right. And I feel the need to receive my best man and matron of honour in the Detention Unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mladic, the Court accepts a waiver without being informed of what you'd rather do than be in court. It's hereby on the record that you waived your right. Therefore, we'll resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, first of all, put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not present in the courtroom and we heard his waiver just before the last break. I have quite a number of items on my agenda, and I saved them for a rainy day. I start with the replacement of P2586. On the 21st of April of this year, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence, via e-mail that a corrected version of P2586 had been uploaded into e-court. The Prosecution requested the Chamber to instruct the Court Officer to replace P2586 with the version uploaded under Rule 65 ter number 30368b. On the 22nd of April, the Defence responded, stating that it did not object. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the existing version of P2586 with the uploaded document. Next item is a remaining issue from the testimony of Vinko Nikolic. On the 5th of February of this year, D893, a table of concordance with regard to the adjudicated facts included in Vinko Nikolic's witness statement was marked for identification, pending verification of the information contained in the document. This can be found at transcript pages 31240 through 31243. As of today's date, the Defence has not verified the information contained in D893. The Chamber sets a deadline of one week from today for the Defence to respond. Next item is a remaining issue from the testimony of Goran Krcmar, P7171. On the 3rd of March of this year, P7171, an UN Security Council document, was marked for identification, pending an agreement between the parties as to the excerpt to be tendered. On the 2nd of April, the Prosecution advised the Chamber via e-mail that: 1, it had informed the Defence of its proposed selection which was uploaded into e-court under 65 ter number 32099a; and, 2, the Defence had not requested the tendering of additional portions. On the 26th of June, the Prosecution sent the Chamber a further e-mail advising that the B/C/S translation of the excerpt had been uploaded into e-court and attached to the English investigation. The question arises whether the Defence has any objections to the admission of the document bearing 65 ter number 32099a. If you are not in a position to respond, Mr. Lukic, and I see you're nodding no, which is hereby on the record, the Chamber is hereby instructing the Registry to assign P7171 to 65 ter number 32099a and admits it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Defence is -- does not need to give specific reasons if they want to revisit the matter by not later than next week, Tuesday. If there are serious portions to be added, Mr. Lukic, then we'll reconsider our decisions without requiring you to give the usual reasons for reconsidering a decision. Four -- number 4 on my agenda is a remaining issue from the testimony of Ian Hanson. It's about D1084. On the 25th of June, 2015, exhibit number D1084 was reserved for two pages of a document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05491. This can be found at transcript page 36339. The Chamber at that time instructed the Defence to upload these pages into e-court and decided these pages will be admitted once uploaded. On the 9th of July, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution via e-mail that the pages had been uploaded under the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D05491a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the extracts to the reserved exhibit number and hereby admits D1084 into evidence. Next is a remaining issue from the testimony of Milutin Misic. It's about D1095. During the testimony of Milutin Misic between 8 and 10 July of this year, translation issues arose with regard to the documents marked for identification D1095, D1096, D1105, and D1106. In the weeks after his testimony, the Defence advised the Chamber and the Prosecution via e-mails that the English translations had been uploaded into e-court under document numbers -- document IDs 1D25-1896, 1D25-2445, 1D25-1762, and 1D25-1906 respectively. With regard to D1105, it concerned a revised translation. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the corresponding translations to D1095, D1096 and D1106 and hereby admits them into evidence, whereby D1096 stays under seal. Lastly, the Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of D1105 with the revised translation and admits D1105 into evidence. Next on my agenda are remaining issues from the testimony from the testimony of Tihomir Stevanovic. I start with the admission of P7372. On the 7th of May of this year, P7372 was marked for identification pending English translation. This can be found at transcript page 35257. On the 24th of July, the Prosecution advised the Chamber via e-mail that an English translation had been uploaded into e-court under document ID 0430-3446-ET-1. On the 11th of August, the Defence advised the Prosecution and the Chamber via e-mail that it had no objection. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation and admits P7372 into evidence. The next is replacement of P2109. On the 6th and the 7th of May of this year, during the testimony of Tihomir Stevanovic, a translation issue arose with Exhibit P2109. This can be found at transcript pages 35225 and 35250. On the 24th of July, the Prosecution advised the Chamber via an e-mail a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0529-6797-ET-1. On the 11th of August, the Defence advised the Prosecution and the Chamber via e-mail that it had no objection. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P2109 with the revised translation. I now move to a remaining issue from the testimony of Drasko Vujic. During the testimony of Drasko Vujic on the 4th of May of this year, P7368, a newspaper article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated the 17th of November, 1995 was marked for identification following the Defence's objection to admission. This can be found at transcript pages 35039 through 35040. The Defence indicated it would address the document during re-examination of the witness. However, the Defence has not made any further submissions on this matter. This can be found at transcript pages 35040 and 35062. The Chamber sets a deadline of one week from today for the Defence to respond. Perhaps it's not much of a response, but at least to make any submission in relation to the admission of this document. I now move to remaining issues from the testimony of Bruno Franjic. The first one is a revised translation of P7433. During the testimony of Bruno Franjic on the 25th of June of this year, the Chamber asked for a review of the English translation of the witness's CV, admitted as P7433. This can be found at transcript page 36384. On the 16th of July, the Prosecution informed the Chamber in an e-mail that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under number doc ID 0687-0517-ET-1 and requested replacement of the existing translation with the revised version. In this revised translation, the description of the witness's occupation as "court sworn criminology expert" has now been corrected to "court sworn forensic criminalistics expert." Does the Defence have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber hereby then instructs the Registry to replace the current the translation of P7433 with the revised translation. Next is the admission of D1085. During the testimony of Franjic on the 29th of June of this year, exhibit number D1085 was reserved for an excerpt from a brochure from Unis Igman d.d. Company to be selected and uploaded by the Defence. This can be found at transcript pages 36486 through -487. On the 29th of July, the Defence advised the Chamber in an e-mail that it had selected pages 1 and 2 of the brochure to be admitted as D1085. On 11 August the Defence informed the Chamber that the excerpt had been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter number 1D05461a and requested its admission into evidence. Any objections from the Prosecution? You have 48 hours to revisit the matter if you suddenly change your mind and wanted to express any objections. But the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the extract as uploaded to the reserved exhibit number and admits D1085 into evidence. And, again, a request for reconsideration doesn't need to be motivated similarly as I -- was the case previous with the Defence. I now to remaining issues from the testimony of Goran Dragojevic. During Goran Dragojevic's testimony on the 14th of May of this year, his 92 ter statement was admitted as Exhibit D1049 together with three associated exhibits. Those are D1050 through D1052. This can be found at transcript pages 35591 and 35619. The Chamber notes that the Defence did not seek admission of the other eight associated exhibits included in its 92 ter motion dated the 15th of September, 2014. Could the Defence indicate whether it still intends to tender these associated exhibits or whether they are withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to revisit the issue and go through the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear from you by next week, Tuesday, and if do you not make any submissions, they are considered to be withdrawn. I move onto admission of P6976. During the testimony of Milorad Sajic, P6976, a video of a meeting in Banja Luka, was marked for identification. Subsequently the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber that a revised English translation of the video's transcript is available. The Defence indicated that it had no objections. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of P6976 with the revised version uploaded as doc ID 0301-0000b-1 and admitted P6976 into evidence. Next item deals with the replacement of a translation and concerns Exhibit P7023. On the 2nd of April of this year, the Prosecution sent an e-mail informing the Defence and the Chamber that a revised English translation of Exhibit P7023, an excerpt of the 49th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, was available under Rule 65 ter number 2410b. The Prosecution indicated that the revised version identifies the speaker as Mr. Karadzic. However, in identifying the speaker, the revised version adds ten pages of the document to the exhibit. Furthermore, it is sufficiently clear from the transcript of the 18th of December, 2014 in this case that the excerpt contains the words of Mr. Karadzic. Under these circumstances, the Chamber denies the Prosecution's request to replace the English translation of P7023. I move to the admission of D1083. On the 23rd of June of this year, D1083 was reserved for an extract of a document describing data and equipment used by the Ljubija mining company. Subsequently, the Defence, in an e-mail, informed the Chamber and the Prosecution that an excerpt had been uploaded under Rule 65 ter number 1D05826. The Chamber instructs the Registry to assign Rule 65 ter number 1D05826 to Exhibit D1083 and admits it into evidence. I would now read an oral decision on the admission of P6889. The Chamber as I said now delivers its decision on the admission of Exhibit P6889 which was marked for identification during the testimony of Nedjo Vlaski on the 4th of November, 2014. This document was further used during the testimony of Tomislav Puhalac on 10th of November. On the 4th of November, the Defence challenged the authenticity of P6889 an undated report on meetings between the SDS Main Board and the Crisis Staff between the 1st of the January and the 31st of May, 1992 and objected to its admission. On the 20th of January, 2015, the Prosecution stated that the parties were in discussion about this document, and on the 6th of March, the Prosecution informed the Chamber by e-mail that the parties had not reached an agreement. The Defence submits that P6889 was created by Bosnian Muslims and not by Serb authorities as Trnovo was at one point under Muslim control. I refer to transcript pages 27821, 27822, 27846 and the OTP e-mail of the 6th of March. The Prosecution submits that the Trnovo security service created this document and that the Sarajevo Agency for Investigation and documentation recovered it during the reintegration process; transcript pages 27821 and -822 and 27844. It further submits that P6889 was created by Serbs on the basis of the references and the language used in the document, as well as its consistency with other documents that reflect similar records of the same meetings, including P3777 and P6887 to be found at transcript pages 27844 and in the e-mail of the 6th of March. The Prosecution noted also that Vlaski at transcript page 27807 confirmed his own comments in those meetings as they were recorded in P6889. The applicable law governing the admission of evidence is set out in Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which allows a chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. Authenticity is a factor to be taken into consideration in determining whether the tendered material has probative value. Definite proof of reliability is not required. Prima facie evidence of reliability on the basis of sufficient indicia is sufficient to grant admission the Chamber has reviewed P6889 in light of the parties' submissions and the testimonies of Vlaski and Puhalac. The Chamber notes that the document bears a signatory body which states, "State Security Sector, Trnovo," and that was a quote, and that the Prosecution provided information on the origin of the document, namely, that it was recovered by the Agency for Investigation and Documentation. P6889 is also largely consistent with other exhibits that describe the same meetings, including P3777 and P6887. Vlaski also described parts of P6889 and thereby implicitly confirmed as accurate the minutes of the meeting as they are recorded in the document. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber finds that there are sufficient indicia for prima facie proof of reliability, that P6889 is relevant and of probative value pursuant to Rule 89(C) and hereby admits it into evidence. The Chamber, however, emphasises that the weight to be attributed to P6889 will be assessed in the context of all the evidence before the Chamber. The Chamber now moves to translation issue that's rose with regard to P6889 during Vlaski and Puhalac's testimonies. This can be found at transcript pages 27863 to 27864 and 28026 to 28027. On the 15th of December, 2014, the Chamber informed the Chamber and the Defence by e-mail that a revised English translation had been uploaded into e-court under document 0228 -- yes. It was the Prosecutor that informed the Chamber on the 15th of December, 2014 that the revised English translation had been uploaded under number 0228-0101-A-ET. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P6889 with the revised translation. Finally, the Prosecution is instructed to file notification containing its e-mail dated the 6th of March, 2015 for the record. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I now move to the replacement and admission of P6865. On the 29th of October, 2014, during the testimony of Slavko Kralj, the Prosecution tendered in intercept bearing 65 ter number 25112 for which the Chamber reserved exhibit number P6865, pending the uploading of a revised translation. On the 24th of July of 2015 the OTP indicated in an e-mail that the revised translation had been uploaded and on the 11th of August, the Defence responded that it did not object to the revised translation. The Chamber therefore instructs the Court Officer to replace the existing translation of P6865 with the translation bearing doc ID number 0504-7165-ET-1 and admits P6865 into evidence. I move to the admission of D649. On the 19th of September, 2014, during the testimony of Witness GRM246, Exhibit D649 was marked for identification pending the outcome of a discussion between the parties concerning its reliability. This can be found at transcript pages 25917 through 25918. However, the Chamber has not received any additional submissions since that time. Could the parties tell the Chamber what the result of that discussion was, if there is any result? And I can imagine that you not be able to do that right way; but if so, you have an opportunity do it now. No one stands up. Therefore, one week from today is the deadline hereby set for additional submissions on the admission of D649. I move to the replacement and admission of P7019. On the 17th of December, 2014, during the testimony of Boro Tadic, Exhibit P7019 was marked for identification due to its illegibility. The Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and Defence on the same day, stating that it had uploaded a more legible version and requesting the replacement and admission of the exhibit. On the 5th of March of this year, the Chamber set a deadline of seven days for any additional submissions once the Registry had replaced the exhibit. On the 7th of March, the Registry filed a memo confirming the exhibit's replacement, after which no additional submissions were made. The Chamber hereby admits Exhibit P7019 into evidence. Next on my list is the admission of P7209. On the 12th of March, 2015, during the testimony of Miso Rodic, Exhibit P7209 was marked for identification pending a English translation. On the 17th of March, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence, indicating that the translation had been uploaded and that it would request replacement of the existing translation and admission of the document into evidence. The question to the Defence is whether it has any objections to admission? I apply the same system, that is, that the Chamber instructs the Court Officer to replace the existing translation of Exhibit P7209 with the translation bearing doc ID number 0091-6545a and admits P7209 into evidence. Until Tuesday, Mr. Lukic, you have an opportunity, and you can do that without motivation, to request the Chamber to reconsider this decision, of course, then giving the reasons why you oppose the -- why you object to the admission. Yes, of course, if you do. I move to the next item, which is also a remaining issue from the testimony of Miso Rodic. On the 12th of March during his testimony, the Defence indicated that the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 18387 which it had tendered as an exhibit associated with Rodic's witness statement was mistakenly referenced in that statement. The Chamber also notes that the document is already in evidence as part of Exhibit P3271. And for these reasons, the Chamber denies the admission into evidence of the document bearing Rule 65 ter number 18387. I move to my next item which deals with the withdrawal of 92 ter motions for dropped witnesses. On the 6th of February and the 25th of March, 2015, the Defence filed submissions informing the Chamber that it was withdrawing several witnesses who could not be called to testify. The Chamber considers, in such circumstances, that the corresponding Rule 92 ter motions for such witnesses are also withdrawn and hereby place this is on the record. I move to a remaining issue from the testimony of Bosko Kelecevic. On the 15th of July of this year, P7485, an interview with Bosko Kelecevic, was admitted into evidence. On the 16th of July, the Prosecution requested via e-mail that P7485 be replaced with an excerpt of the interview which has been uploaded into e-court as document bearing 65 ter number 32715b. The question to the Defence is whether there's any objection to this replacement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is shorter version. Probably not, but maybe we should just be given some time to see if we want to include anything for better understanding purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, would it be a problem for you if I would do it in a similar way, to already instruct and if you revisit the matter by next Tuesday that you don't have to give -- of course, you would have to give the reason why you want to revisit it, but you don't have to motivate why reconsideration is justified. Then the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace P7485 with the document bearing 65 ter number 32715b. I move to the semi-last item which is about D745. On the 5th of November, 2014, during the testimony of Nedjo Vlaski, the Prosecution stated it did not object to the admission of D745 as long as the Defence provided information relating to the source of the document and established personal knowledge foundation through the witness. On the 20th of May of this year, the Defence e-mailed the Chamber and Prosecution and advised that Vlaski: "Confirmed that the document was provided to him by the Serbian security level." On the 15th of July, the Chamber asked the Prosecution for its position. As at today's date the Prosecution has not responded, and the Chamber therefore sets a deadline of one week for the Prosecution to provide its submissions. The very last item, D768.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be sure that the record will be even more perfect than it is already, page 45, line 17, reads that Vlaski had confirmed that the document was provided to him by the Serbian -- let me now check. "By the Serbian security service." I now really move to my last item, D768. During the testimony of Cedo Sipovac on 12 November 2014, D768 was marked for identification pending translation and use with another witness. The translation issue was resolved on the 3rd and the 24th of February, 2015. On the 12th of March, D768 was tendered through Miso Rodic and, on the same date, a new translation arose, and therefore D768 remained marked for identification. It was about failing translation or missing translation of handwriting in that document. Thereafter, the Chamber asked the Defence four times - on the 10th of April and the 30th of April via an e-mail, and on the 14th of May and the 8th of July in court - for an update on the progress of the revised translation. Can the Defence inform the Chamber within one week of the progress of the revised the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can do that now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever I expect you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with my Case Manager he sent this for revised translation to CLSS and they were not able to see what we were asking from them although it is partially visible on the document and I think that the witness also read it on the transcript that it was instead of Croatian it was Yugoslav nationality of this man. So we can accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If the parties -- you'll understand that I don't have it on the top of my head available at this moment. Could the parties seek an agreement that on some handwriting is missing, that the parties agree on what it is and most likely that would be what the witness read it to be, and that the parties are satisfied that the translation of what the witness read in court is correctly to be found in the transcript in the English transcript. If could you agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll -- Mr. Lukic and I will speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll speak to each other. And then we'd like to hear from you by not later than next week. And that would celebrate the fifth occasion on which the matter was raised. I'm not going to congratulate you on that, Mr. Lukic, especially because I understand that you sent it for translation but there were some problems. Is there anything the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.text: If I may be the first, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.text: Yes, there is a deadline for the Defence to respond to P7510 and it's the map of Vlasenica in regard of elevation lines, and we cannot respond today.

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... it's quite simple elevation lines connect points which are at the same elevation and by looking at them thoroughly, you can see where the hills are and where it goes down. And usually the map explains what is the difference in altitude between two lines and often on every 50 or 100 metres, you would find somewhere on that line what altitude, what elevation, that line presents.

utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But since there were some issues in regard of obstacles, those obstacles could be seen on this bigger map as well.

utterances.text: Okay. That's promising that you may have others as well. One second, please.
